ledger.claim_text: The SR-71 Blackbird operational cruising altitude was approximately 85,000 feet at Mach 3.2 (over 2,100–2,200 mph).
ledger.source_title: Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird Flight Manual (TO 1SR-71A-1) / NASA Dryden Technical Reports
ledger.publisher: United States Air Force / NASA Dryden Flight Research Center
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Operational ceiling exceeded 85,000 ft with standard cruise speed between Mach 3.17 and Mach 3.2.

ledger.claim_text: The moveable inlet spike translates rearward by up to 26 inches (66 cm) at Mach 3 to control internal conical shockwaves and decelerate air to subsonic speeds (Mach 0.5) before the compressor face.
ledger.source_title: NASA Technical Note D-6397: Performance of an Axisymmetric Mixed-Compression Inlet at Mach 3
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: The translating spike moves mechanically back up to 26 inches depending on Mach number, capturing the normal shock in the diffuser throat.

ledger.claim_text: An inlet unstart occurs when the terminal shockwave is violently expelled out the forward duct within milliseconds, causing an instantaneous loss of engine thrust and sudden high drag.
ledger.source_title: NASA TM-86737: Flight Evaluation of an Inlet Unstart Detection and Recovery System on the SR-71
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Expulsion of the internal normal shock wave ('unstart') results in massive duct pressure surge, immediate loss of thrust, and huge nacelle drag.

ledger.claim_text: The sudden asymmetric thrust and drag during an unstart produced violent yaw and roll forces that could slam the pilot's helmet against the cockpit canopy.
ledger.source_title: Sled Driver: Flying the World's Fastest Jet / Skunk Works Memoirs
ledger.publisher: Smithsonian Air & Space Magazine / Brian Shul
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Pilots recounted severe head strikes against the canopy window during violent yaw unstarts before the digital automatic recovery system (DAFICS) was implemented in the 1980s.

ledger.claim_text: At Mach 3.2 cruise, the Pratt & Whitney J58 turbo-ramjet's inlet compression system generated over 70% to 80% of the entire propulsion unit's net forward thrust.
ledger.source_title: The J58 Engine and Its Bleed Bypass Design: Propulsion for the Blackbird
ledger.publisher: Aircraft Engine Historical Society / Pratt & Whitney Technical Heritage
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: At Mach 3.2, approximately 80% of total system thrust was generated by pressure recovery in the inlet diffuser and ejector nozzle, with the core turbojet acting primarily as a gas generator for the ramjet effect.

ledger.claim_text: Atmospheric skin friction heated the titanium fuselage to between 500°F and over 600°F (with leading edges exceeding 800°F), requiring expansion joints that wept fuel on the tarmac but sealed tight under Mach heat expansion.
ledger.source_title: Lockheed Skunk Works: A Personal Memoir of My Years at Lockheed / Ben R. Rich
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Fuselage expanded several inches in flight; JP-7 fuel tanks were designed without rubber bladders due to temperature extremes, sealing as thermal expansion took up tolerances.

ledger.claim_text: Over approximately 4,000 surface-to-air missiles fired at the SR-71 during its active military service, zero aircraft were lost to enemy weapons, with tactical doctrine relying on high-altitude acceleration.
ledger.source_title: SR-71 Blackbird: Stories, Tales, and Legends / Paul F. Crickmore
ledger.publisher: National Museum of the United States Air Force / Osprey Publishing
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: USAF records confirm over 4,000 missile launches (including SA-2 and SA-5 systems) without a single loss to hostile fire.
